title: How Tibo copies crowded markets to build a $1M MRR portfolio
summary: Tibo argues bootstrapped founders should skip "blue ocean" invention and instead rebuild an existing product for the user the market leader ignores. He gives a three-question framework for picking where to compete and cites Mark Pincus's repeat-copy playbook.

principles.text: Don't hunt for untouched markets. Pick a crowded market and serve the user type being ignored.
principles.quote: I didn't find new, untouched markets. I found crowded markets with one type of user being ignored and built something better for them.

principles.text: Blue-ocean invention suits VCs who can absorb 99 losses, not bootstrappers with limited attempts.
principles.quote: For you as a founder, if your number of attempts is limited, one loss can be dramatic.

principles.text: Ask what the best version looks like for the person the market leader ignores.
principles.quote: What does the best possible version of this look like for the person being ignored by the current market leader?

principles.text: Only pursue problems people already pay to solve; no payers means insufficient pain.
principles.quote: Who is already paying for a solution to this problem? If nobody is paying, the problem is not painful enough. Full stop.

principles.text: Find the gap every leader leaves: segments they ignore because they are too big or focused elsewhere.
principles.quote: Every market leader ignores someone. They get too big, too bloated, too focused on a certain kind of client. That gap is where you live.

principles.text: Define the one thing that would make that user switch immediately, and be meaningfully better at it.
principles.quote: What would make that person switch today? Not eventually. Immediately. That's your one thing to be meaningfully better at.
